| [THEORY-017](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-017.md) v7 | In a Hilbert-space model only unitarily invariant structure is intrinsic; a basis or tensor factorisation, and so any parts or features, is extra data supplied from outside the space, and the record's Hilbert-space works differ in where they get it | Carroll (2021), [LIT-123](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-123.md): a quantum theory is fixed up to unitary equivalence by the Hamiltonian's spectrum, and subsystems come from a factorisation that the dynamics must select. Van Rijsbergen ([LIT-262](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-262.md)) computes only traces and inner products, and treats each observable's eigenbasis as a "point of view". DisCoCat's ε/η composition ([LIT-273](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-273.md)) is orthogonally covariant, while its Frobenius sequel ([LIT-272](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-272.md)) stipulates a basis and composes by elementwise product in it. [THEORY-004](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-004.md) is the same point for learned representations. This is a synthesis across the four, not a result any one of them states. | [THEORY-261](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-261.md) v3 | In sparse distributed memory, recall of uniform random data from exact cues is a signal-to-noise problem whose optimum activates about (2MT)^-1/3 of the hard locations, and capacity then grows in proportion to the number of hard locations, rising toward about a tenth of them at 0.999 bit fidelity, not with the word length | Kanerva (1992), [LIT-921](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-921.md), §§3.5–3.7, read in full in [NOTE-779](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-779.md), after Jaeckel (1989a). | [THEORY-361](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-361.md) | When every object but one has full grade in exactly one of two attribute-sorted lists and the one has full grade in both, finding it under min takes at least about half the objects' worth of accesses for any algorithm that only reads the lists from the top and looks up objects already seen, and, with the tied objects in random order, about as many in expectation even for algorithms that may look up any object; a query on one attribute alone costs k accesses whatever the number of objects | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md): Example 6.3 and Theorem 6.4, the paper's proof that no algorithm is instance optimal once lucky lookups are allowed. | [THEORY-363](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-363.md) | For finding the top k objects under a monotone combining function from m lists each sorted by one attribute, with sorted and random accesses the only costs, the threshold algorithm is correct and on every database costs at most a constant times what any correct algorithm that makes no wild guesses costs; the constant is m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, no deterministic algorithm does better when the function is strict, and once wild guesses are allowed no algorithm has such a guarantee on databases with ties | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md). For every monotone combining function it is instance optimal among correct algorithms that make no wild guesses (Theorem 6.1), with ratio m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, tight for strict functions (Corollary 6.2, Theorem 9.1). It is a guarantee relative to a class of algorithms under an access-cost model. | [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md) v4 | In one study of a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data, each element's top layer drawn geometrically, greedy search on uniform random data in 8 dimensions needed a number of distance computations that grew no worse than logarithmically with the number of items and stayed below a single-layer navigable graph's at every size tested, and in 4 dimensions the beam width needed for a fixed recall saturated; the logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which the index does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the measured growth departs from it | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) from arXiv v4. For the graphs it does build, cost no worse than logarithmic is measured on uniform random data at d = 8, a saturating beam width at d = 4, and at d = 128 (200M SIFT) the growth departs from a logarithm. A proof for the graphs HNSW builds is QUESTION-187. The paper gives no worst-case bound and no recall guarantee. Construction is argued to cost about N searches. | Active |
| [THEORY-366](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-366.md) | With a fixed number of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance divided by its mean tends to zero, the farthest point comes within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest with probability tending to one; independent coordinates meet this condition, while data on a low-dimensional subspace, or queries that fall inside well-separated clusters, escape it | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft (1999), [LIT-1099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1099.md), read in [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) from the authors' 1998 technical report. IID coordinates and several correlated or non-identical workloads satisfy the condition; a diagonal line, two latent degrees of freedom and queries inside clusters do not. The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The result concerns the ratio of distances at fixed n, and does not show that real high-dimensional data loses contrast, or that indexes fail. | Active |

| [THEORY-369](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-369.md) v2 | Under uniformly distributed, independent data and queries in the unit cube with Euclidean distance and a fixed number of points, an optimal nearest-neighbour search over any index that partitions points into blocks or convex clusters of at least two points must read a fraction of blocks that grows toward all of them as dimension rises; with a five-fold sequential advantage for scanning, estimates put the crossover at about 15–26 dimensions for rectangular and spherical bounding regions, and two tree indexes measured on 50,000 points lost to a scan beyond about 10 | Weber, Schek and Blott (1998), [LIT-1107](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1107.md), read in [NOTE-919](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-919.md). Under uniformity and independence, with the expected nearest-neighbour distance used as every query's radius and integrals evaluated by Monte Carlo, the fraction of blocks read passes the 20% line at about d = 15–20 for rectangular regions and 26 for spherical ones. | [THEORY-370](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-370.md) | On an n × n lattice whose nodes also get long-range links drawn with probability proportional to lattice distance to the power −r, a searcher that knows only the target's position and the links of nodes already reached delivers in expected time polylogarithmic in n only at r = 2: greedy routing then takes O((log n)²) steps, while for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such searcher needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))), even at r = 0 where short paths exist | Kleinberg (2000), [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), read in [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md). The upper bound is proved only for one local and one long-range link per node; the k-dimensional statement (r = k) is asserted, not proved; the family is inverse power laws of a distance every node can compute, so it does not show that no other link structure is navigable. | Active |
| [THEORY-372](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-372.md) | For c-approximate near-neighbour search over n points in Euclidean space, space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} are achievable on any data set whenever c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1) (c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1) in Hamming space), and no list-of-points structure, the model of known data-independent hashing, does better on random instances; without that model the curve is matched only at query time n^{o(1)} by one or two cell probes | Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn and Waingarten (2017), [LIT-1120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1120.md), read in [NOTE-918](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-918.md) from the arXiv full version. | [THEORY-376](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-376.md) v3 | In a simulated single-client, read-only database answering selection queries on one relation, describing cached data by the predicates of past queries let each query be answered partly from cache, with only the remainder Q ∧ ¬V sent to the server; this matched page caching on a clustered index, beat it on an unclustered one, and, on an unindexed attribute with a disk cache, answered over 60% of 1% queries without contacting the server; the cost of computing probe and remainder queries was not charged | Dar, Franklin, Jónsson, Srivastava and Tan (1996), [LIT-1113](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1113.md), read in [NOTE-904](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-904.md). | [THEORY-384](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-384.md) | A nearest-neighbour graph built by pruning each point's links against all other points with a factor α > 1, so that from every point some link is α times closer to any other point, lets greedy search from any start reach a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps of cost O((4α)^d log ∆), for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by one on n, and the build takes O(n³) time done naively | Indyk and Xu (2023), [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md), read in [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md). | [THEORY-385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-385.md) v3 | In HNSW over 10-dimensional data in 100 isolated clusters, linking each new item to its nearest neighbours leaves part of the bottom layer unreachable from the entry point and caps recall well short of 1 however wide the query search, while linking a candidate only when it is nearer the new item than to any neighbour already kept keeps that layer connected and reaches recall near 1 with about half the links; on uniform data at 10 and 64 dimensions the two rules differ little; shown in Malkov and Yashunin's own tests on 10 million points and in an independent re-run on 30,000, which found the nearest-neighbour rule capped at a recall@10 of 0.72 to 0.83 against 0.999, at matched build cost too | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md). In HNSW, each new element's neighbours are chosen either as its M nearest candidates or by a pruning rule that keeps a candidate only if it is nearer the new element than to any neighbour already kept, a rule related to the relative neighbourhood graph. On 10M random d = 10 vectors in 100 isolated clusters, nearest-neighbour links failed to reach high recall and the pruning rule did not. In every test reported, the rule was at least as good. Its gain was largest at low dimension, at high recall, and on clustered data, and small on uniform or very high-dimensional data. These are the authors' benchmarks: one clustered dataset, synthetic, with no independent replication in this reading. Re-run independently at smaller scale on promotion (2026-10-20), with the same result. | Active |
| [THEORY-388](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-388.md) | Locality-sensitive hashing answers approximate near-neighbour queries over n points with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, where ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) is set by how much more often near pairs collide than far ones and is at most 1/(1+ε) for approximation 1+ε in Hamming space, with constant success probability per query; the paper gives upper bounds only and proves no limit on what organizing can buy | Indyk and Motwani (1998), [LIT-1106](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1106.md), read in [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) from the authors' 1999 expanded version, compared with the STOC text. A hash family under which points within r1 collide with probability at least p1 and points beyond r2 with at most p2 gives n^ρ random tables, each storing every point: O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space and O(n^ρ) hash evaluations per query, ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2), for the decision version, which ring-cover trees connect to approximate nearest neighbour with polylog overhead. Bit sampling gives ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in Hamming space and, by embedding, ℓ_p for p in [1, 2]; the STOC text states 1/ε and only for ε > 1. Grid bucketing gives Õ(d) queries for n·O(1/ε)^d preprocessing. Preprocessing is counted as space. Nothing is proved about whether these exponents can be beaten. | Active |

| [THEORY-697](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-697.md) | Sparse distributed memory's read weights each stored pattern by the number of hard locations within the read radius of both query and pattern, a ball-intersection count that falls roughly exponentially in Hamming distance over a local window, so softmax attention over cosine similarity of unit-norm queries and keys, with a fitted inverse temperature, approximates the SDM read there; the approximation cannot hold globally, since the binary count vanishes beyond twice the radius, and its inverse temperature comes from a regression, not from the paper's analytic bound | Bricken & Pehlevan (2021), [LIT-269](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-269.md), read in full in [NOTE-242](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-242.md), which re-evaluated the intersection formula and the fit. The authors name "Retrieval Collapse", a two-stage failure in which (1) AI-generated content comes to dominate search results, eroding source diversity, and (2) low-quality or adversarial synthetic content enters the retrieval pipeline. On 1,000 MS MARCO queries, each with ten Google-retrieved web documents (Original Pool), they add GPT-5-nano documents one per round for 20 rounds (pool contamination 0% → 66.7%), in two scenarios: an "SEO" pool (LLM rewrites of original documents with high-IDF keywords) and an "Abuse" pool (clickbait drafts with named entities and numbers falsified). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1677](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1677.md) | Brown (2025) argues that recommender systems bear on authenticity in two opposed ways: by ranking content on behavioural signals that cannot reveal users' second-order desires they foster volitional misalignment by design, while by showing users whom they behave like they can prompt self-understanding, a benefit that opacity threatens, so that recommenders serve authenticity only if they are controllable and explain which similarity relation drove each recommendation. | Étienne Brown, read in [NOTE-1792](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1792.md) (Read). Brown argues that recommender systems affect users' capacity to be their authentic selves, both negatively and positively. He offers a "minimal", multi-dimensional account of authenticity with two dimensions: volitional alignment (Frankfurt, via Rings: acting on first-order desires one reflectively endorses at second order) and self-understanding (an epistemic dimension, relational rather than purely introspective: others' testimony and recommendations are a source of self-knowledge). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1695](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1695.md) | Scalco, Gesualdo, Cerqueti and Cinelli (2026) propose detecting information voids as statistically anomalous periods in which online information demand (searches, page views), rescaled to its own mean, exceeds supply (posts, news volume), and report for COVID-19 vaccines in six European countries that such voids clustered at rollout and regulatory events, outlasted periods of overabundance, and coincided with a lower share of highly credible sources and a higher share of low-credibility ones among shared links. | Scalco, Gesualdo, Cerqueti and Cinelli (2026), read in [NOTE-1748](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1748.md) (Read). Treating the online information ecosystem as a market with information **demand** (Wikipedia page views, Google Trends) and **supply** (Facebook posts via CrowdTangle, Twitter full-archive, GDELT news volume), the authors rescale each series by its mean, define an information delta δt = ŝt − d̂t, decompose δ by STL and flag remainder outliers by an IQR rule. Anomalies with δ < 0 are **voids** (demand far exceeds supply), δ > 0 **overabundance**; a five-regime scale runs Void / Lack / Balance / Abundance / Overabundance. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1697](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1697.md) | Davoudabadi, Makui and Rasouli (2026) propose a recommender that combines a user score built on a peak-end reference point and prospect-theory gains and losses with an organizational score based on the gap between the organization's projected and desired operational state, weighting the organization more as the user's purchase history is more diverse and the user more as the organization has slack, and in a simulation of one manufacturer with 100 synthetic users it reduces workshop over- and under-utilization relative to purely customer-driven recommendation. | Davoudabadi, Makui and Rasouli, read in [NOTE-1740](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1740.md) (Read). The authors propose a recommender that scores each candidate item for a user by combining (a) a user-side score and (b) an organization-side score. User side: a reference point built from the user's peak and most recent purchase utilities (peak-end rule), item distances to it split into gains and losses with a prospect-theory-style value function (the EXPTODIM method), and a "user flexibility" index from the diversity of the user's past purchases. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1701](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1701.md) | Montero-Porras, Smets and Lenaerts show that in a two-population replicator model of a platform that rewards costly quality content and creators who invest in it, quality and its absence are both stable, the platform needs far more creators investing than creators need the platform to reward them, and a temporary rise in the payoff to promoting cheap content that lasts long enough moves the system into decline that restoring the original payoff does not undo. | Montero-Porras, Smets and Lenaerts (2026), Enshittification of Algorithmic Recommendation: An Evolutionary Model of Platform-Creator Dynamics, read in [NOTE-1787](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1787.md) (Read). A two-population evolutionary game between a platform (x = probability its recommender rewards costly quality content) and creators (y = probability a creator invests in quality), under replicator dynamics: ẋ = x(1−x)(Ry−A), ẏ = y(1−y)(Vx−C). With R > A and V > C there are two stable pure equilibria, (1,1) "virtuous" and (0,0) "vicious", separated by an interior saddle at (x*, y*) = (C/V, A/R). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1705](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1705.md) | Hu, Jagadeesan, Jordan and Steinhardt prove that, in a model where non-myopic, discounting producers choose content every round and a platform recommends by a standard no-regret online-learning algorithm (LinHedge or LinEXP3), equilibrium producer effort and user welfare vanish over time under typical learning-rate schedules, because a slow learner makes today's effort move future recommendations too little to repay its cost; algorithms that permanently stop recommending producers whose content falls below a threshold sustain constant effort, and individualized criteria that make producers specialize recover near-optimal welfare in limiting cases | Incentivizing High-Quality Content in Online Recommender Systems (Hu, Jagadeesan, Jordan, Steinhardt), read in [NOTE-1774](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1774.md) (Read). A game-theoretic model of a recommender platform that runs an online-learning (adversarial linear contextual bandit) algorithm, recommending one producer per arriving user, while P non-myopic, discounting producers choose a D-dimensional content vector at every step, paying cost \|\|p\|\|^c and earning 1 when recommended. Content quality is measured as producer effort \|\|p\|\| and as user welfare E[<u, p>]. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1708](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1708.md) | Burke et al. argue that recommender systems should be evaluated by the outcomes they produce for each stakeholder group (consumers, providers, upstream, downstream, the platform and third parties), with metrics derived from each group's values and goals, and that the resulting multidimensional scores may be left unaggregated or combined by weights, constraints, Pareto-frontier distance or learned expert orderings, there being no single correct way to quantify the values involved. | Burke et al. (2025), De-centering the (Traditional) User: Multistakeholder Evaluation of Recommender Systems, read in [NOTE-1793](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1793.md) (Skimmed). A position-and-guidance article. Recommender evaluation has been almost wholly about the end user; a multistakeholder evaluation assesses "the quality of recommendations ... across multiple groups of stakeholders". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1712](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1712.md) | Adler argues that pornography's move since 2007 to ad-supported, algorithm-driven tube sites controlled by one near-monopoly firm makes it a Big Tech speech-platform problem: recommendation, rigid categorization, search-term optimization and data-driven commissioning shape both what users come to want and what producers make, conforming content to the platform's categories and mainstream viewing habits. | Adler (2024), Arousal by Algorithm, read in [NOTE-1776](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1776.md) (Read). Adler argues that since 2007 pornography has moved onto ad-supported, algorithm-driven "tube sites", mostly owned by one near-monopoly firm (MindGeek, renamed Aylo in 2023), and should be analysed as a "Big Tech" speech-platform problem. Recommendation, rigid categorization, keyword/search optimization and data-driven commissioning of content constrain what users see, shape their preferences, and shape what producers make. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1728](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1728.md) | Thorne et al. (2018) built a dataset of 185,445 claims derived by altering Wikipedia sentences, with independent annotators labelling each claim against Wikipedia as supported, refuted or not verifiable and recording the evidence sentences (Fleiss κ 0.68) | The central account of [LIT-2301](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2301.md), read in [NOTE-1873](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1873.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1736](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1736.md) | Park et al. (2023) give LLM agents a memory stream of timestamped natural-language observations, retrieved by a sum of recency, importance and relevance scores, plus periodic reflections that cite the memories they are inferred from and are stored back into the stream, and find in an ablation rated by human judges that memory, reflection and planning each add to the believability of agent behaviour, with errors coming from failed retrieval and embellishment rather than from memories being absent | The central account of [LIT-2492](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2492.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1887](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1887.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1744](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1744.md) | Salemi et al. report that, for LLM agents answering data-science questions over large file collections, a main agent that broadcasts requests to a blackboard and lets file-holding helper agents decide whether to respond outperforms a matched design in which the main agent assigns subtasks to named helpers, in end-to-end accuracy and in file-discovery F1, with the advantage growing with the size of the collection, at roughly 1.8× the per-question cost. | The central account of [LIT-2470](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2470.md), read in [NOTE-1852](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1852.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1745](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1745.md) | - **Sentence**: Song, Cheng, Zhou and Wang (2022) model the argumentation of scientific papers as a knowledge graph of typed argumentation units (claim, warrant, backing, rebuttal and others) linked by intra-article relations and citation-based inter-article relations, build one by hand from twelve papers on technology acceptance, and use it to display how claims evolved from TAM to TAM2 and TAM3, without evaluating that use. - | The central account of [LIT-2515](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2515.md), read in [NOTE-1812](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1812.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1767](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1767.md) | Jiménez Gutiérrez et al. report that indexing a corpus as a schemaless entity graph extracted by an LLM and retrieving passages by Personalized PageRank seeded from query entities improves single-step multi-hop retrieval over dense retrievers on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, matching iterative retrieval (IRCoT) at a fraction of its cost, and that new knowledge can be integrated by adding edges rather than re-summarizing. | The central account of [LIT-2485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2485.md), read in [NOTE-1858](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1858.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1771](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1771.md) | - **Sentence**: Xu et al. (2025) propose A-MEM, an agent memory in which an LLM writes each new memory as a Zettelkasten-style note, links it to similar earlier notes and rewrites those notes' descriptions in place, and report that it outperforms fixed-structure memory baselines on long-conversation question answering, most on multi-hop questions, at lower token cost, with link generation and memory evolution each contributing in ablation. - | The central account of [LIT-2502](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2502.md), read in [NOTE-1857](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1857.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1781](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1781.md) | - **Sentence**: Edge et al. (2024) propose GraphRAG, which answers whole-corpus questions by summarizing a hierarchy of communities in an LLM-extracted entity graph and combining the community answers, and report that LLM judges prefer its answers to vector RAG's on comprehensiveness and diversity, while claim-based measures find no significant difference from map-reduce summarization of the source text, over which its advantage is lower token cost. - | The central account of [LIT-2501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2501.md), read in [NOTE-1874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1874.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1783](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1783.md) | - **Sentence**: Jaradeh et al. (2019) present the Open Research Knowledge Graph, which represents a paper's research contribution as a graph relating its research problem, method and results with unconstrained user-chosen properties so that contributions can be compared across papers, and report from twelve authors' sessions that authors are willing to describe their contributions in structured form, leaving versioning, discussion and the representation of knowledge evolution to future work. - | The central account of [LIT-2510](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2510.md), read in [NOTE-1818](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1818.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
